newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania plans tough budget during IMF visit.
newsitem.headline: Romania plans tough budget during IMF visit.

text.p: Romania's centrist government presses on this week with pledges to underpin tough monetary policies by presenting a responsible 1997 budget during a visit by an International Monetary Fund mission.

A government statement said mission chief Poul Thomsen met Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea on Tuesday to assess early steps in an ambitious reform package, focusing on faster privatisation and reshaping of the bloated communist-era industry.

As the team began its evaluation of Romania's progress ahead of a Fund board meeting this month, the government rushed to approve a bank privatisation bill, one of several keys to restoring IMF credits suspended last year.
Parliament is to open debate on the budget on Thursday and the large centrist majority is expected to adopt it quickly.
"I have promises from the (leftist) opposition that they will create no difficulties," Finance Minister Mircea Ciumara told the daily Cronica Romana. "I am optimistic."
Ciumara described the budget as responsible after it was approved by the government last month.
Reforms have been limited during seven years of leftist administration since the fall of communist rule and Ciorbea has repeatedly said they are crucial to win new foreign investment.
Seven years of post-communist rule attracted only $2.3 billion in foreign direct investments, one-tenth of the level in neighbouring Hungary.
Tuesday's government statement said Thomsen acknowledged that "fiscal, budgetary and monetary steps taken so far by the government had positive effects on the functioning of the markets".
Ciorbea's cabinet, seeking about $400 million in IMF loans, has prepared a standard letter of intent to be discussed at a Fund Executive Board meeting in Washington on April 23 and 24.

The 1997 budget deficit is forecast at 4.5 percent of gross domestic product, down from last year's 5.8 percent. That figure was nearly three times higher than the target set by the former leftist government.
The IMF and World Bank suspended credits to Romania last year after the leftists, later ousted in last November's elections, had overshot spending and restricted foreign exchange markets.
Recent statistics paint a far from clear picture of trends within the economy.
Industry recovered in February after two months of falling output but lower exports kept the trade deficit high at $134.5 million in January.
Monthly inflation is seen easing to up to 12 percent for March after hitting a 45-month peak of 18.8 percent in February. It is scheduled to be cut to 2.2 percent by the end of 1997.

Price rises on staple items and utilities have sapped domestic demand, depressing retail trade. Purchasing power fell by 10.8 percent year-on-year in February, while unemployment rose to 7.2 percent of the workforce in March from 6.1 at the end of 1996.
Tough monetary policies have restored confidence in the leu currency after deposit rates climbed to an annual 150 percent from 55 in the New Year.
The removal of foreign exchange market curbs in February also helped to stabilise the leu near 7,000 to the dollar after it plunged to an all-time low of 9,000.
Equity trading, slow in 1996, gained vigour this year with fresh foreign investment flows and greater local interest expected to boost its performance.
